title: Cell Identity and Signaling
text: Cell Identity and Signaling (CIS) Project Summary The Cell Identity and Signaling (CIS) Research Program aims to achieve the following key scientific objectives: (1) advance understanding of critical molecular mechanisms underlying cell identity and signaling; (2) apply this foundational knowledge to uncover key steps in the carcinogenesis cascade; and (3) utilize these insights to create new, mechanism-driven strategies to prevent or block hallmarks of cancer. Cancer cells, through genetic and epigenetic alterations, exploit normal cellular processes of cell growth regulation, differentiation, and embryonic development to their advantage. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the fundamental mechanisms of cell identity and signaling using advanced techniques, innovative cellular and animal models, and model organisms. The CIS investigators supported by both CIS program funds and PICR resources and collaborators are equipped to drive foundational scientific discoveries and translate them into innovative cancer solutions, utilizing advanced technologies in drug discovery, computational cancer biology, RNA therapeutics, cancer modeling, and immunotherapeutics. There are four key research themes shaping CIS: (1) model systems, (2) epigenetics and cell signaling, (3) RNA biology and therapeutics, and (4) computational oncology. During the previous funding cycle, CIS has successfully fostered highly collaborative, cancer-relevant studies that link CIS program themes with other Purdue Institute for Cancer Research (PICR) programs while providing training opportunities for trainees and emerging scientists. Examples of such collaborative studies include: (1) leveraging model organisms to advance cancer research; (2) leveraging computational tools to accelerate cancer pathway and drug discovery; (3) and translating basic findings into cancer solutions by developing innovative RNA-Based therapeutics or drug repurposing. Based on these research areas of strength and the emerging areas of interest pursued by CIS laboratories, the specific aims for the next funding cycle (2025-2030) are to advance the discovery of molecular, epigenetic, and signaling mechanisms that drive cancer hallmarks and identify novel therapeutic targets; leverage and integrate advances in omics-based AI and computational biology to dissect cancer hallmarks and enhance drug repurposing; and dissect the complex interplay between inflammation, microbiome, and genome function in cancer risk and therapy response. These aims collectively drive advancements in basic cancer research by leveraging cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) models and investigating the role of inflammation and the microbiome in cancer progression to drive the discovery of novel and effective treatments while reducing comorbidities and adverse events. This comprehensive approach is expected to enhance basic innovations while improving patient outcomes.

title: Biostatistics for Research in Genomics and Cancer
text: This training grant clearly has major relevance in public health as it is designed to train the next wave of biostatistical researchers in cancer genomics, which is one of the largest and growing areas of biomedical research, in which the demand for well trained biostatistical researchers is much greater than the supply.

title: Quantifying Motor Network Dynamics to Predict and Enhance Outcomes in Pediatric Dystonia
text:
Childhood dystonia profoundly affects children and their families, yet treatment remains limited by the absence
of objective, brain-based biomarkers to guide therapy. This project will leverage advanced neurophysiological
signal analyses and machine-learning methods to identify potential biomarkers that inform deep brain
stimulation decisions and enhance clinical care. By deepening our understanding of motor network dysfunction
and moving these insights toward personalized treatment strategies, this research directly supports the NINDS
mission to reduce the burden of neurological disease and improve quality of life.

title: Cancer Immunology: Across Space & Time
text:
Cancer Immunology: Across Space & Time will address critical gaps in our understanding of the dynamic and
evolving nature of immune surveillance in cancer. By assembling an interdisciplinary faculty and audience in a
retreat-style venue, the conference will advance public health by fostering collaboration, disseminating cutting-
edge science, and supporting early-career researcher engagement.

title: PERM1, a new therapeutic target for PRDM16-associated cardiomyopathy
text:
PRDM16 associated cardiomyopathies occurs in patients with chromosome 1 deletion syndrome and in patients
carrying de novo variants of this gene. We and others showed that female patients who lost PRDM16 develops
cardiomyopoathy at early age and are more likely to die from it. In this proposal, we will provide new knowledge
on why loss of PRDM16 leads to early and more severe cardiomyopathy in females and test whether PERM1
gene delivery improves cardiomyopathy and enhance survival in patients with PRDM16 loss.

title: Investigating the cell intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms governing lung cancer cell plasticity
text:
The ability to dynamically switch cell states enables cancer cells to adapt to environmental and therapeutic
challenges, however, the molecular mechanisms that cancer cells employ to maintain or switch states have not
been fully characterized. This proposal aims to dissect the cell-intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms underlying
lung cancer cell plasticity by leveraging a newly developed single-cell lineage tracing technology. A
comprehensive understanding of these mechanisms will reveal key gene networks that regulate tumor evolution,
and could potentially inform rational therapeutic approaches.

text:

title: Deconstructing the Genetic Basis of Complex Trait Variation
text:
In the past decade, thousands of genetic associations with diverse human complex traits and diseases have
been discovered, yet translating these findings into an understanding of trait or disease biology has remained
challenging. Toward this goal, in this project, we propose to develop new approaches to identify key trait-
relevant genes and explore their interaction with other genetic and environmental factors. Additionally, we will
study how these biological insights can inform and improve disease prediction from genetic data.

title: A multimodal approach to increase accuracy and generalizability in lung cancer early detection
text: Annual use of low-dose CT (LDCT) and Lung-RADs for reporting and managing of LDCT findings reduces lung cancer mortality but is imperfect with frequent false positives and negatives and eligibility criteria that miss many lung cancers. Advances in artificial intelligence, specifically computer vision and machine learning, have enabled accurate detection of lung cancer prior to visible radiographic disease through imaging and circulating DNA assays. This research program aims to test a multimodal approach for lung cancer prediction under the hypothesis that integrating clinical, lung imaging, and circulating DNA fragmentomic features will have greater accuracy and generalizable benefit than current standard of care LDCT screening.

title: Neurodevelopmental Trajectories Associated with Prenatal Cannabis Exposure
text:
Cannabis use during pregnancy has increased substantially, in conjunction with legalization and decreases in
the percentage of the population who believe cannabis use is harmful. In this longitudinal study, we collect
follow-up MRI brain imaging measures at 6 and 18 months of age to complement behavioral assays being
conducted at these same timepoints under the parent project. This work will provide a more comprehensive
approach to identifying early manifestations of atypical neurodevelopment associated with gestational cannabis
exposure.

title: Enhancing untargeted metabolite elucidation by machine learning of fragmentation in mass spectrometry
text:
This project develops open-source artiﬁcial intelligence tools to identify the chemical structures of unknown
metabolites from mass spectrometry data. By improving accuracy, reliability, and scalability of metabolite
annotation, the research will enable the discovery of biomarkers and pathways underlying human diseases. The
resulting computational resources will accelerate biomedical research and support the development of new
diagnostics and therapies.

title: Systematic and scalable phenotyping of mouse mutants for neuropsychiatric disease genetics
text:
The Washington University Scalable Mouse Assay Center (WU-SMAC) for the SSPysGene consortium aims to
comprehensively investigate the impact of genetic mutations linked to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric
disorders, such as autism and schizophrenia, using a large collection of specialized mouse lines. By analyzing
behavior, brain anatomy, and molecular changes, we seek to understand how these mutations influence brain
function and behavior, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms of these complex disorders

title: Molecular Basis for Myelodysplasia Induced by U2AF1 Mutations
text:
Mutations in the RNA splicing gene U2AF1 are commonly observed in Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). In
this proposal, we will define the roles of U2AF1 mutations and co-occurring epigenetic mutations in the
pathogenesis of MDS, and determine the molecular mechanisms of myelodysplasia induced by U2AF1
mutants. Results from these studies may lead to identification of new therapeutic approach for treatment of
MDS.

title: 1/3 Understanding PTSD through Postmortem Targeted Brain Multi-omics
text:
The prevalence of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression are among the most common of the
severe major psychiatric disorders. There have yet to be postmortem studies of well-matched cases and controls
to leverage the fact that these are arguably among the best understood psychiatric disorders in terms of neural
circuit regulation. Building on impactful linked R01 project, in our renewal proposal we will expand the sample
size and dive deeper with more detailed analyses of the postmortem phenotypes and more comprehensive mo-
lecular studies to identify pathways harboring potential diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Effects of Systemic Disease on Corneal Epithelial Pathophysiology
text:
An intact corneal epithelium is one of the most important determinants of clear vision. It is also among the most
common targets of blinding eye disease. The overall goal of this proposal is to define the role of mitochondria
in corneal epithelial homeostasis and determine how we can reverse the blinding effects of corneal epithelial
disease by reestablishing mitochondrial function.

title: Deconstructing nuclear speckles contribution to muscle stem cell activation across lifespan
text:
The regulation and ability of adult stem cells to maintain quiescence and differentiate after injury are strongly
linked to ability to regulate gene expression programs. The role of nuclear speckles in these processes remains
unknown and as such, the focus of this proposal is to build a systems-level understanding of nuclear speckles
and their influence on splicing, transcriptional regulation and stem cell function across lifespan.

title: Systemic Mediators and Biomarkers of Injury in Preterm Infants with Intermittent Hypoxemia
text:
Preterm infants (~0.4 million born in the US yearly) are at risk for frequent blood oxygen drops (Intermittent
Hypoxemia (IH)) that are linked to multiple short- and long-term neonatal morbidities leading to both lifelong
impairments and increased burden on health care cost. Our study investigates both markers and mechanisms
of brain injury from increased intermittent hypoxemia in preterm infants. These data will contribute to our
understanding of brain injury from intermittent hypoxemia and identify potential targets for developing treatments
in the future to improve IH and associated impairments.

title: Predicting Tissue Specific Gli3 Regulatory Activity Using Hand2
text:
Relevance to Public Health
Craniofacial malformations are among the most common congenital defects affecting the human population.
Understanding how gene regulation is controlled and impacted during normal and pathological craniofacial
development is essential for providing better therapeutic interventions and improve human health.

title: Investigating Sex-Specific Hypothalamic Pathology and Immune Infiltration in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
The hypothalamus is responsible for maintaining many processes, such as sleep behavior, metabolism, and
hormonal signaling, that are disrupted in Alzheimer’s disease. This project will investigate how hypothalamic
pathology and neuroinflammation may contribute to underlying mechanisms of sex differences in AD.
Understanding mechanisms of immune infiltration and neuroinflammation in the hypothalamus and how they
may promote sex disparities in AD will inform the development of targeted therapeutics and enable better clinical
interventions across the spectrum of AD severity.

title: Advanced Analysis of High-Resolution Cardiac Diffusion Tensor Images
text:
In this K-25 award, I plan to use prior training in biomedical engineering and material science to now focus on
medical imaging of the heart. Specifically, we will be using a technique know as diffusion tensor imaging to
better understand how the cells in the heart are arranged. The goals of this grant are to facilitate my scientific
growth in medical imaging and machine learning and to provide mechanism for me to develop the necessary
skills to become and independent investigator.
